cards.front: Cardiac output equals {{c1::heart rate times stroke volume}}.
cards.back: A ventricle that fills more ejects more (the Frank-Starling relation).
cards.quote: cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume, and a ventricle that fills more ejects more (the Frank-Starling relation)

cards.front: On a graph of flow against right atrial pressure (Pra), why does the circulation settle where the heart's rising line crosses the veins' falling line?
cards.back: Left of the crossing, return exceeds output, so blood collects in the right atrium and Pra climbs. Right of it, the heart sends on more than returns, so Pra falls. Either way Pra moves to the crossing.
cards.quote: From either side, Pra moves toward the crossing.
cards.section: A first look at the two lines

cards.front: When a change moves only the veins' line (blood volume, venous tone, resistance to venous return), cardiac output and right atrial pressure go {{c1::the same way}}.
cards.back: The new crossing slides along the heart's line, which slopes up.
cards.quote: Move the veins' line (blood volume, venous tone, resistance to venous return) and output and atrial pressure go the same way.
cards.section: A first look at the two lines

cards.front: Why does a change that moves only the heart's line (a stronger or weaker heart) send cardiac output and right atrial pressure in opposite directions?
cards.back: The new crossing must still lie on the unmoved veins' line, and that line slopes down: more flow comes only at lower Pra, less flow at higher Pra.
cards.quote: When the heart's line moves, you slide along the veins' line, which slopes down, so they go opposite ways.
cards.section: A first look at the two lines

cards.front: In the two-line model of cardiac output and venous return, how do you predict a change that moves both the heart's line and the veins' line?
cards.back: Work out each shift in turn. Where both push a number the same way, it moves that way; where they push it opposite ways, the larger shift wins.
cards.quote: Where the two shifts push a number the same way, it moves that way; where they push it opposite ways, the larger shift wins.
cards.section: A first look at the two lines

cards.front: A transfusion raises mean systemic filling pressure in a person whose heart is already very full, so the operating point sits on the flat top of the heart's line. Predict the change in right atrial pressure and cardiac output.
cards.back: Right atrial pressure rises; cardiac output stays about the same.
cards.why: The veins' line slides right, so the crossing slides along the heart's line. The same-direction rule holds only on sloping parts; where the heart's line is flat, output stays put.
cards.quote: The rule holds for one change at a time, once the first few seconds of mismatch have passed, on the sloping parts of both lines.
cards.section: A first look at the two lines

cards.front: What is the mean systemic filling pressure (Pms)?
cards.back: The single pressure the systemic circulation settles at once the heart is stopped and flow has ceased: the zero-flow pressure.
cards.quote: That zero-flow pressure is the mean systemic filling pressure (Pms).
cards.section: The stretched store: mean systemic filling pressure

cards.front: {{c1::Stressed}} volume stretches vessel walls and generates recoil pressure; unstressed volume fills vessels without stretching them.
cards.quote: Stressed volume stretches the walls and generates recoil pressure.
cards.section: The stretched store: mean systemic filling pressure

cards.front: With the heart stopped, why is there still a pressure (Pms) in the systemic vessels?
cards.back: Blood beyond the unstressed volume stretches the vessel walls, and their elastic recoil is the pressure. It is wall stretch, not the height of the blood.
cards.quote: In the vessels too, it is the stretch of the walls, not the height of the blood, that makes the pressure.
cards.section: The stretched store: mean systemic filling pressure

cards.front: A lumped systemic circulation has compliance 0.2 L per mmHg and stressed volume 1.4 L. A transfusion adds 0.6 L, all of it stressed. What is the new mean systemic filling pressure?
cards.back: Pms = stressed volume / compliance. Before: 1.4 / 0.2 = 7 mmHg. After: (1.4 + 0.6) / 0.2 = 2.0 / 0.2 = 10 mmHg.
cards.quote: Each 0.2 L of stressed blood adds 1 mmHg.
cards.section: The stretched store: mean systemic filling pressure

cards.front: How does sympathetic venoconstriction raise mean systemic filling pressure without adding any blood?
cards.back: It lowers venous capacitance, turning unstressed volume into stressed volume, so more blood stretches the walls. This moves the veins' line, not the heart's.
cards.quote: It lowers capacitance, the volume held at a given pressure, and turns unstressed into stressed volume without adding blood.
cards.section: The stretched store: mean systemic filling pressure

cards.front: In an intact circulation, cardiac output and right atrial pressure change together. How did Guyton's group, in anaesthetized open-chest dogs, measure how venous return depends on right atrial pressure?
cards.back: They bypassed the right heart with an external pump into the pulmonary artery, so the experimenters set Pra and measured the flow returning from the body.
cards.quote: The experimenters, not the heart, set Pra, and they measured the flow returning from the body.
cards.section: Guyton's dogs: set the atrial pressure, read the return

cards.front: In Guyton's open-chest dogs, why did venous return stop rising once right atrial pressure fell to about -2 to -4 mmHg?
cards.back: Veins collapse when the pressure inside falls below the pressure around them, and a collapsed vein limits flow, so the veins' line goes flat: no unlimited suction.
cards.quote: Veins collapse when the pressure inside falls below the pressure around them, and a collapsed vein limits flow however low the downstream pressure goes.
cards.section: Guyton's dogs: set the atrial pressure, read the return

cards.front: In the lumped model, venous return Qvr = {{c1::(Pms - Pra) / Rvr}}.
cards.back: Pms is mean systemic filling pressure, Pra right atrial pressure, Rvr resistance to venous return. Return is zero when Pra equals Pms.
cards.quote: Set b + k x Pra = (Pms - Pra) / Rvr.
cards.section: Worked problem 1: find the operating point

cards.front: On the venous return curve, what does lowering resistance to venous return (Rvr) do, and what stays fixed?
cards.back: The line tilts steeper about its zero-flow point, which stays at Pms, so more blood returns at every Pra below Pms.
cards.quote: A change in Rvr tilts the line about its zero-flow point at Pms: a lower Rvr makes it steeper, so more returns at every Pra below Pms.
cards.section: Guyton's dogs: set the atrial pressure, read the return

cards.front: In a made-up right-heart bypass study, set right atrial pressure and steady venous return are: 6 mmHg, 1.0 L per min; 3 mmHg, 2.5; 0 mmHg, 4.0; -3 mmHg, 5.5; -6 mmHg, 5.6. Using the straight part and Qvr = (Pms - Pra) / Rvr, find Pms and Rvr.
cards.back: Straight part: flow rises 1.5 L per min per 3 mmHg fall, slope 0.5 L per min per mmHg, so Rvr = 2 mmHg min per L. Zero flow is 2 mmHg above 6: Pms = 8 mmHg. The -6 point sits on the collapse plateau.
cards.quote: Pms is where the line meets zero flow.
cards.section: Guyton's dogs: set the atrial pressure, read the return

cards.front: Name two pumps outside the heart that aid venous return.
cards.back: Contracting leg muscles squeezing deep veins against their valves, and spontaneous inspiration lowering intrathoracic pressure.
cards.quote: Contracting leg muscles squeeze deep veins against their valves (skeletal muscle mechanics), and spontaneous inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure (lung mechanics and surfactant).
cards.section: Guyton's dogs: set the atrial pressure, read the return

cards.front: What three factors set how high the cardiac function curve (output against right atrial pressure) sits?
cards.back: Contractility, heart rate (only while each beat still has time to fill), and afterload.
cards.quote: How high it sits depends on contractility (the strength of contraction at a given preload)
cards.section: Where the pump meets the veins

cards.front: Illustrative model: heart Qc = 2 + 1 x Pra (L per min, Pra in mmHg); veins Qvr = (Pms - Pra) / Rvr with Pms = 8 mmHg and Rvr = 1 mmHg min per L. Find the operating point.
cards.back: Set 2 + Pra = 8 - Pra, so 2 x Pra = 6 and Pra = 3 mmHg. Q = 2 + 3 = 5 L per min. Check: (8 - 3) / 1 = 5.
cards.quote: Set them equal (at the crossing, the heart pumps what the veins return).
cards.section: Worked problem 1: find the operating point

cards.front: A positive inotrope strengthens contraction; blood volume, venous tone and resistance to venous return are unchanged. Predict the steady-state changes in cardiac output and right atrial pressure.
cards.back: Output rises and right atrial pressure falls.
cards.why: Only the heart's line lifts, so the crossing slides up the unmoved, downward-sloping veins' line. A stronger pump moves more blood on at every Pra and draws the atrium down.
cards.quote: A stronger pump moves more blood on at every atrial pressure, so it draws the atrium down.
cards.section: Worked problem 1: find the operating point

cards.front: Guyton read right atrial pressure as a back-pressure that limits venous return; others read it as a consequence of pump flow. Where do the two readings agree, and where do they differ?
cards.back: Both fit the same two lines and give the same operating point. They differ on what happens in the first seconds after a change.
cards.quote: Both readings fit the same two lines and give the same operating point, so for predicting where the circulation settles they agree.
cards.section: Worked problem 1: find the operating point

cards.front: A ventilator raises the pressure in the chest around the heart. Right atrial pressure rises. Does the ventricle necessarily fill more? Explain.
cards.back: No. It can fill less.
cards.why: Stretch depends on pressure across the heart wall (Pra minus surrounding pressure) and ventricular stiffness. Raising chest pressure can raise Pra while lowering transmural pressure.
cards.quote: So raising chest pressure, as a ventilator does, can raise Pra while the ventricle actually fills less.
cards.section: Worked problem 1: find the operating point

cards.front: In the linear model (baseline Pms 7 mmHg, Pra 2 mmHg, output 5 L per min, compliance 0.2 L per mmHg), a patient loses 0.4 L of stressed blood. Which line moves, and where do output and right atrial pressure go?
cards.back: The veins' line slides left (Pms falls to 5 mmHg). Sliding down the heart's line, both fall: output 4 L per min, Pra 1 mmHg.
cards.quote: A loss of 0.4 L does the reverse, down to 4 L per min and 1 mmHg.
cards.section: Moving the operating point

cards.front: In the linear model (Pms 7 mmHg, Rvr 1, heart Qc = b + Pra with b = 3), contractility suddenly falls to b = 1. Predict the immediate steady-state output and right atrial pressure.
cards.back: Output falls from 5 to 4 L per min and Pra rises from 2 to 3 mmHg.
cards.why: Only the heart's line drops, so the crossing slides down and right along the veins' line: opposite directions.
cards.quote: Q falls from 5 to 4 L per min and Pra rises from 2 to 3 mmHg.
cards.section: Heart failure: one line, then both

cards.front: In systolic heart failure, what raises mean systemic filling pressure over seconds, and what over hours to days?
cards.back: Seconds: reflex venoconstriction recruits stressed volume. Hours to days: renal retention of sodium and water adds blood volume.
cards.quote: Reflex venoconstriction can recruit stressed volume within seconds, and over hours to days renal retention of sodium and water (water, sodium and potassium) adds blood volume.
cards.section: Heart failure: one line, then both

cards.front: In the linear model, compensated heart failure (b = 1, Pms 9 mmHg) restores output to 5 L per min; a positive inotrope (b = 5, Pms 7) raises it to 6. Why does only the first raise the risk of edema?
cards.back: Compensation restores output by moving the veins' line, so Pra rises (to 4 mmHg) with higher upstream venous and capillary pressures. The inotrope moves the heart's line, so Pra falls (to 1 mmHg).
cards.why: Same-direction versus opposite-direction rule for which line moves.
cards.quote: with higher upstream venous and capillary pressures that favour edema
cards.section: Heart failure: one line, then both

cards.front: Linear model of compensated heart failure: heart Qc = 1 + Pra, veins Qvr = (9 - Pra) / 1. Fluid is removed until Pms falls to 8 mmHg, with the heart unchanged. Find the new Pra and output, and state the trade-off.
cards.back: 1 + Pra = 8 - Pra, so Pra = 3.5 mmHg and Q = 4.5 L per min. Atrial (and upstream) pressure falls, but output falls too: both move the same way because only the veins' line moved.
cards.quote: Together they raise Pms, sliding the veins' line right.
cards.section: Heart failure: one line, then both

cards.front: A model circulation has mean arterial pressure 95 mmHg, right atrial pressure 5 mmHg, mean systemic filling pressure 10 mmHg and cardiac output 5 L per min. Calculate total peripheral resistance and resistance to venous return.
cards.back: TPR = (MAP - Pra) / Q = (95 - 5) / 5 = 18 mmHg min per L. Rvr = (Pms - Pra) / Q = (10 - 5) / 5 = 1 mmHg min per L.
cards.quote: Rvr is not total peripheral resistance (TPR): TPR = (MAP - Pra) / Q, with mean arterial pressure (MAP) upstream.
cards.section: Resistance: which vessels?

cards.front: Why does arteriolar dilation move both the veins' line and the heart's line?
cards.back: It lowers resistance to venous return, tilting the veins' line steeper, and lowers afterload, which can lift the heart's line. Output rises; Pra can go either way.
cards.quote: It lowers Rvr, tilting the veins' line steeper, and lowers afterload, which can lift the heart's line.
cards.section: Resistance: which vessels?

cards.front: A drug causes venodilation only (veins relax, arterioles unchanged). Predict the change in mean systemic filling pressure, cardiac output and right atrial pressure.
cards.back: Pms falls, the veins' line slides left, and output and right atrial pressure both fall.
cards.why: Increased capacitance stores blood; only the veins' line moves, so output and Pra go the same way.
cards.quote: Venodilation lowers Pms: the veins' line slides left.
cards.section: Resistance: which vessels?

cards.front: Linear model: heart Qc = b + Pra, veins Qvr = (7 - Pra) / Rvr. Arteriolar dilation halves Rvr from 1 to 0.5. How large must b become for right atrial pressure to stay at its baseline 2 mmHg, and what is output then?
cards.back: Pra = (Pms - Rvr x b) / (1 + Rvr x k): (7 - 0.5b) / 1.5 = 2, so b = 8 and Q = 8 + 2 = 10 L per min. The heart's lift must match the tilt; with less lift, the tilt wins and Pra rises.
cards.quote: Output rises, and Pra can go either way; in the table's last row the tilt outweighs the lift, and Pra rises from 2 to 3.33 mmHg.
cards.section: Resistance: which vessels?

cards.front: By the Fick principle, cardiac output = oxygen uptake / {{c1::arterial minus mixed-venous oxygen content}}.
cards.back: At steady state, oxygen taken up by the lungs leaves in the blood flowing through them.
cards.quote: At steady state, the oxygen the lungs take up each minute leaves in the blood flowing through them.
cards.section: The Fick principle

cards.front: Why must the Fick calculation use oxygen content and not oxygen saturation?
cards.back: Content (mL O2 per L, bound plus dissolved) is a volume of oxygen per litre. Saturation is a percentage and holds no volume of oxygen.
cards.quote: A saturation will not do: it is a percentage and holds no volume of oxygen.
cards.section: The Fick principle

cards.front: Mixed-venous blood for the Fick method is sampled in the {{c1::pulmonary artery}}.
cards.back: It is venous blood from the whole body after mixing, drawn through the distal lumen of a pulmonary artery catheter.
cards.quote: Mixed-venous blood is venous blood from the whole body after it has mixed, sampled in the pulmonary artery through the distal lumen of a pulmonary artery catheter.
cards.section: The Fick principle

cards.front: Oxygen uptake is 250 mL O2 per min, arterial content 200 mL O2 per L, pulmonary artery content 150 mL O2 per L, and an arm vein holds 100 mL O2 per L. Compare the correct Fick output with the output from the arm-vein sample.
cards.back: Correct: 250 / (200 - 150) = 5.0 L per min. Arm vein: 250 / (200 - 100) = 2.5 L per min, half the true value, because the arm extracts more than the body average.
cards.quote: An arm vein reports only what the arm extracted, not what the whole body extracted.
cards.section: The Fick principle

cards.front: What three assumptions does the direct Fick method make?
cards.back: Steady state, no intracardiac shunt (pulmonary and systemic flow equal), and a true mixed-venous sample.
cards.quote: The direct method assumes steady state, no intracardiac shunt (so pulmonary and systemic flow are equal) and a true mixed-venous sample.
cards.section: The Fick principle

cards.front: By indicator dilution, Q = amount injected / {{c1::area under the first-pass concentration-time curve}}.
cards.quote: Q = amount injected / area under the first-pass concentration-time curve
cards.section: Indicator dilution

cards.front: In indicator dilution, why does a higher cardiac output give a smaller area under the concentration-time curve?
cards.back: Faster flow dilutes the dye more and clears it sooner, so concentration is lower and lasts less time.
cards.quote: Faster flow dilutes the dye more and clears it sooner, so the area under the concentration-time curve is smaller.
cards.section: Indicator dilution

cards.front: 10 mg of dye is injected into a central vein. The first-pass concentration-time curve downstream has an area of 100 mg s per L. What is cardiac output in L per min?
cards.back: Q = 10 mg / 100 mg s per L = 0.1 L per s. x 60 = 6.0 L per min.
cards.quote: Units: the area is concentration times time (mg s per L), so mg divided by mg s per L leaves L per s.
cards.section: Indicator dilution

cards.front: During an indicator-dilution measurement, some dye leaves the blood before reaching the sampling site. Predict whether the calculated cardiac output is too high or too low, and why.
cards.back: Too high. Less dye passes the sampler, so the area is smaller, but the calculation still divides the full injected amount by it.
cards.why: The method assumes no indicator is lost from the blood.
cards.quote: It assumes complete mixing, no indicator lost from the blood, and recirculation excluded (the downslope is extrapolated before the second pass).
cards.section: Indicator dilution

cards.front: How does pulmonary artery thermodilution measure cardiac output?
cards.back: A cold crystalloid bolus is injected into the central venous circulation and temperature is read in the pulmonary artery: cold replaces dye.
cards.quote: it injects a cold crystalloid (salt solution) bolus into the central venous circulation and reads temperature in the pulmonary artery
cards.section: Indicator dilution

cards.front: An adult at rest, at steady state with no shunt, has oxygen uptake 300 mL O2 per min, arterial content 190 mL O2 per L and mixed-venous content 130 mL O2 per L. Heart rate is 100 beats per min. Find cardiac output and stroke volume.
cards.back: Difference 190 - 130 = 60 mL O2 per L. Q = 300 / 60 = 5.0 L per min. Stroke volume = 5,000 / 100 = 50 mL per beat.
cards.quote: Stroke volume. At 80 beats per min, 5,000 / 80 = 62.5 mL per beat.
cards.section: Worked problem 2: measure the output

cards.front: In an anaesthetized pig whose right heart is replaced by an external pump, how could you test whether right atrial pressure acts as a back-pressure on venous return?
cards.back: Raise Pra without touching the pump (e.g. raise airway pressure), with blood volume fixed and flow recorded beat by beat. If caval flow falls immediately, Pra acts as a back-pressure there; this shows transients, not the cause in an intact person.
cards.quote: If raising Pra at fixed pump speed immediately lowers caval flow, Pra acts as a back-pressure here.
cards.section: Design problem: cause or consequence?

cards.front: A new cuff's blood pressure readings correlate with an arterial line at r = 0.95 across patients, but read 8 mmHg high on average. Can the cuff replace the arterial line?
cards.back: Not as an absolute measure. The readings correlate (rise and fall together) but do not agree (one cannot stand in for the other value for value).
cards.why: Correlation is not agreement, as with a thermometer that always reads 3 degrees high.
cards.quote: Correlation says two measures rise and fall together; agreement says one can replace the other (a thermometer reading 3 degrees high correlates perfectly with a true one).
cards.section: Tracing the curve with the chest closed

cards.front: Van Loon and colleagues (2020) estimated Pms in ventilated pigs from inspiratory holds and compared it with the pressure after ventricular fibrillation. What did they conclude about the hold value?
cards.back: It correlated strongly with the stop-flow pressure but was not interchangeable: a dynamic characteristic of the circulation, not an absolute measure of volume state.
cards.quote: The authors concluded that the hold value is a dynamic characteristic of the circulation, not an absolute measure of volume state.
cards.section: Tracing the curve with the chest closed
